title: Pfeffernüsse
subtitle: German spiced peppery nut biscuits rolled in icing sugar
excerpt: Pfeffernüsse are small, round German spiced biscuits with a distinctive peppery warmth from black pepper alongside cinnamon, cloves, and mixed spice. You get about 40 compact biscuits, each rolled in icing sugar while still warm so the coating clings. Watch the size: roll them small so they bake through evenly.
sourceNotes: Pfeffernüsse (pepper nuts) are a traditional German and Scandinavian Christmas biscuit, documented in German confectionery records from the 17th century. The defining characteristic is black pepper in a spiced dough. The icing-sugar coating is the standard finishing method in the German tradition.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the baked biscuits before rolling in icing sugar. Roll in icing sugar after defrosting.
recipe.batchNotes: The dough keeps refrigerated for up to 3 days. Roll and bake in batches.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Pfeffernüsse improve over 2 to 3 days as the spices develop. Store in an airtight tin; roll in a second coating of icing sugar before serving if the first coat has been absorbed.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 180 degrees Celsius. Fan oven: 165 degrees Celsius. Middle shelf.

glossaryTerms.definition: A biscuit made with multiple warming spices, typically including cinnamon, cloves, and black pepper in the German tradition. The spice blend is what distinguishes Pfeffernüsse from a plain butter biscuit. Ground almonds in the dough add richness and a slightly tender crumb.

The method of rolling warm biscuits in icing sugar immediately after baking. The residual warmth and slight stickiness of the biscuit surface allows the icing sugar to cling in a thin, powdery layer. Rolling while warm gives a better coating than rolling once cooled; the icing sugar can be refreshed with a second roll before serving.

Warm the butter, honey, and soft brown sugar in a medium saucepan over low heat, stirring until the butter has melted. Remove from the heat and leave to cool for 10 minutes.

Beat in the egg. Sift together the flour, bicarbonate of soda, cinnamon, mixed spice, black pepper, and cloves, then add to the honey mixture along with the ground almonds. Stir to a firm dough. Chill for 30 minutes.
Preheat the oven to 180 degrees Celsius. Line two baking trays with baking paper.
Roll the chilled dough into small balls of about 12 g each (roughly the size of a cherry). Place on the prepared trays, leaving 3 cm between them. The balls will spread slightly.
Bake for 10 to 12 minutes until the biscuits are firm at the base and set but not deeply coloured on top. They should feel firm when you press the side gently.

Remove from the oven. Leave to cool for 3 to 4 minutes on the tray, then while still warm, roll each biscuit in the icing sugar to coat all over. Transfer to a cooling rack. Once cooled, roll in icing sugar a second time for a thicker coating.

attrs.problem: The icing sugar coating melts into the biscuit rather than sitting as a white powder
attrs.avoid: Avoid rolling the biscuits in icing sugar when they are still piping hot; the surface moisture dissolves the sugar.
attrs.fix: Wait 3 to 4 minutes after removing from the oven before rolling. The biscuits should be warm but not steaming. If the coating is absorbed, let the biscuits cool fully and roll in a second layer of icing sugar.

attrs.problem: The biscuits spread too much and are flat rather than round
attrs.avoid: Avoid rolling balls that are too large; bigger balls take longer to set in the oven and spread more.
attrs.fix: Keep the balls small, around 12 g each. If they spread significantly, chill the remaining dough for a further 15 minutes before rolling and baking the next batch.

attrs.problem: The biscuits are very hard after cooling
attrs.avoid: Avoid storing in an open tin or uncovered; these biscuits dry out quickly.
attrs.fix: Store in an airtight tin. If the biscuits are already very hard, place a half-slice of bread in the tin overnight; the moisture from the bread softens the biscuits.
